C031.label: Australia · 1943 · Threepence (3d)
C031.notes: SER OC-AU-001. George VI · IND:IMP still in legend (Emperor of India — pre-1948 drop). Reverse: three wheat stalks · AUSTRALIA · THREE PENCE · 1943 · S. Country #10. Wartime: Australia needed silver change, US mints helped. Pocket money from a Pacific-war economy — melt, not face. Junk Ag = melt (see SILVER.md). SER siblings: OC-AU-002 (1944 Perth penny) · OC-AU-003 (1966 platypus 20¢). Australia flips now 3.
C031.story: A 1943 Australian threepence, struck in the middle of World War II. King George VI is on the front, and the back shows three stalks of wheat by George Kruger Gray, a design used since 1938 — before the war began. It's made of real silver, which is why it feels different from today's coins in your hand.

C345.year_line: 2008 · Mint: none on the portrait side
C345.metal: copper-nickel (75% copper, 25% nickel) · 5.66 g · 23.6 mm · Reeded
C345.design: obverse 4th portrait bust of Elizabeth II right wearing tiara · ELIZABETH II AUSTRALIA · reverse superb lyrebird displaying plumage · 10 · Stuart Devlin / Ian Rank-Broadley
C345.label: Australia · 2008 · 10 Cents
C345.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Obverse: ELIZABETH II and AUSTRALIA around the Rank-Broadley portrait with the designer's IRB below the bust; the date sits at the bottom and reads 2008 when followed in legend order around the rim (the digits base to the rim, so they present reversed left-to-right in the photo — read digit by digit in an enlarged, contrast-enhanced crop). Reverse: big 10 over the fanned tail of the superb lyrebird. Matches the collection's existing AU.X.10-cents type (2006 strike, C295) exactly in portrait and design; the 1966 first-year type is a different portrait generation and is filed separately in the collection.
C345.story: An Australian 10 cents from 2008, the everyday silver coin with the superb lyrebird fanning its tail across the back — the bird that can mimic almost any sound it hears, drawn here feather by feather. The front carries Queen Elizabeth the Second in Ian Rank-Broadley's portrait, the one Australia used from the late 1990s until the Queen's death. The lyrebird design by Stuart Devlin has been on the 10 cents since decimal currency began in 1966. The collection already holds a 2006 strike of this same coin; this 2008 joins it as a second year.

C349.year_line: 1977 · Mint: Royal Australian Mint (Canberra); no mint mark on this issue
C349.label: Australia · 1977 · 50 Cents
C349.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Obverse: ELIZABETH II and AUSTRALIA around the Machin portrait on a twelve-sided flan; the date sits after AUSTRALIA at the lower right. Reverse: 50 CENTS and SILVER JUBILEE around a central starburst ringed with 25 small emblems, read off the photo in legend order. The year is design-locked: this Silver Jubilee reverse was struck for one year only, 1977, so the commemorative design itself settles the date even where individual digits sit soft in the photo. The twelve-sided planchet, Machin portrait and Jubilee reverse together admit no other Australian 50 cents issue.
C349.mint: Royal Australian Mint (Canberra); no mint mark on this issue
C349.story: An Australian 50 cents from 1977, struck for Queen Elizabeth the Second's Silver Jubilee — twenty-five years on the throne. It is a big twelve-sided coin. The front shows the young Queen in Arnold Machin's famous portrait, the one Australia used through the sixties and seventies. The back is a celebration wreath: a shining starburst in the middle ringed by small emblems, with the words SILVER JUBILEE and 50 CENTS around them. It was designed by Stuart Devlin, the goldsmith behind most of Australia's first decimal coins, and it was made to be kept — but plenty slipped into change anyway.
